I am seventy-nine years old, and I have worked this land since I was a boy. My father taught me, and now my bones know the rhythm of the seasons better than my mind does. My wife and I still farm our 4.1 mu together. It is not much, but it is ours, and our well gives us water when the sky does not.

My wheat went into the ground last October, as it always does. It is greening up now, so the first thing I will do is spread urea when the wheat revives—about 8 jin per mu—to wake it up properly. I will irrigate three times this spring and summer: once at green-up, once at jointing, and once during grain filling. I always use improved wheat seed, and I plough the field with the rotary tiller before planting every autumn. I will spray herbicide once and insecticide twice; that is enough if you catch the timing right. I expect around 900 jin per mu from the wheat if the weather holds.

After we harvest the wheat in early June, I will plant hybrid maize the same week. I do not plough for the maize anymore—I learned years ago that no-tillage works just fine, and at my age it saves me days of back-breaking work. I will put down compound fertilizer at planting and then topdress with urea when the maize reaches the big trumpet stage. I will irrigate twice, which is usually sufficient with the summer rains, and I will spray for pests three times. The hybrid seed is dear, but it gives me good grain. I hope for about 1,000 jin per mu from the maize.

We are only two old people now, so I keep things simple. I do not chase the highest yield at any cost. I use what I have learned over seventy years: steady water, timely fertilizer, and do not let the weeds or insects get ahead of you.
